extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; policymakers, legislators, and legal scholars interested in principles of liberty and state action
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for when individuals or the State may be constrained or must act—covering harm-based limits on liberty, duties to others (including children), the role of education, and how government should be organised and intervene. The text offers principles and practical prescriptions for balancing individual freedom and state action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm-based limitation on liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should be free to act in matters concerning only themselves; the only legitimate basis for exercising power over a person against their will is to prevent harm to others or protect the rights of third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State should not interfere in purely self-regarding actions except where those actions injure others. Examples and discussion emphasise that liberty is grounded in individual good and autonomy, but limited where third-party rights are at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on alienating one's fundamental liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: A person should not be permitted to alienate their fundamental freedom (e.g., selling oneself into slavery); freedom cannot be interpreted as permitting an act whose consequence is permanent loss of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The slavery example shows limits of contractual freedom: engagements that permanently forfeit liberty are voidable because they negate the very presumption in favour of voluntary choice. Such acts defeat the justification for allowing voluntary disposition in the first place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited enforceability of personal-service contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts involving personal relations or services ought not to be legally binding beyond a limited duration; personal relations (notably marriage) have qualities that make perpetual legal enforceability questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baron von Humboldt's view is cited: engagements of a personal nature should not be enforceable indefinitely; Mill notes moral and third-party consequences complicate but does not fully accept a blanket rule. The guidance indicates legal limits should respect the peculiar nature of personal-service relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to consider reliance and induced expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person, by promise or conduct, causes another to rely on continued conduct (creating expectations and life plans), new moral obligations arise toward that person which cannot be ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill acknowledges these obligations may not require fulfilment at all costs, but they must be weighed before retracting conduct. This functions as a constraint on unilateral withdrawal from engagements that others have relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty to regulate private power over others (family relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State must vigilantly control any private power individuals exercise over others (e.g., husbands over wives, parents over children) and extend legal protection equally to those subject to private power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family relations often escape adequate state oversight; Mill argues wives should have the same rights and legal protection as others, and that the State should not permit absolute parental/despotic control when it injures those subject to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory basic education up to a standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The State ought to require and compel education up to a certain minimum standard for every citizen (e.g., ensure ability to read and acquire a basic general knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instrument: public examinations beginning early, annual renewals, fines or other penalties for neglectful parents (with provision to make good the child's education at parent's expense). The aim is to secure minimum literacy/knowledge for social functioning and prevent children being born into wretchedness by parental neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content limits for state-mandated examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations required by the State should, beyond instrumental skills, be confined to facts and positive science; disputed subjects (religion, politics) should be tested only on who holds such opinions and why, not on their truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-branch examinations should be voluntary. The State may ascertain and certify knowledge required to make conclusions worth attending to, but must avoid using examinations to impose doctrinal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State support versus State direction in education
rubrics_metrics.description: The State may require education and assist in funding or providing it, but should not monopolise or exclusively direct education; state education should be one among competing experiments rather than the sole moulding instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues for diversity of education to preserve individuality of character. The State's role can include funding poorer children or providing examples, but central direction risks a despotism over the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates should certify, not legally restrict
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees and public certificates should be awarded to all who pass examinations, but such certificates should not legally exclude individuals from professions or confer special legal advantages beyond public opinion's weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving governments the power to exclude people from professions based on alleged deficiency; certification should attest ability without being used as an instrument of exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objections to government interference (decision criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering government action that is not about restraining liberty, three objections should be weighed: (1) individuals may do it better than government; (2) doing it privately may serve as civic education and development; (3) enlarging government functions increases state power and risks dependency/tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objections guide when the State should undertake beneficial actions: prefer individual or voluntary organisation where feasible; preserve spaces for citizens' practical political education; avoid unnecessary expansion of governmental power that creates bureaucratic dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of decentralisation of power, centralisation of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange public administration so as to have the greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency, while centralising information and diffusing it from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical model: localities run local business and are accountable to constituents; a central organ collects and shares experience and general principles, compels conformity to laws, but refrains from micromanaging. This balance preserves local initiative while leveraging central knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central superintendence limited to information and law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The central authority's role should be to concentrate experience and information, advise, and ensure local officers obey laws, but not to substitute central administration for local judgment in matters not covered by general rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central organ should have the right to know local actions and to make available knowledge from elsewhere; its coercive powers should be limited to cases of overriding national interest. The Poor Law Board is cited as an example of appropriate central superintendence when mismanagement has national spillover effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of principal national ability within the bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not concentrate the country's principal talents and occupations entirely within government offices, since this risks creating a large, dependent bureaucracy and diminishes opportunities for external cultivation of governance ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the State monopolises desirable careers, ambition and talent will focus on bureaucratic advancement; the bureaucracy then becomes powerful and self-protecting. Maintain independent institutions and careers so ability outside government can criticise and refresh public administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of government action when private provision is absent
rubrics_metrics.description: When private enterprise or voluntary associations cannot provide certain necessary services or institutions (e.g., in very backward societies), the State may legitimately undertake them as the lesser of two evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include State undertaking schools, universities, joint-stock companies when private capacity does not exist. Such intervention should be limited to necessities and abandoned when private provision becomes feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral duty concerning procreation and marriage regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing children into existence without reasonable prospects of providing for their physical and mental needs is morally wrong; laws restricting marriage when parties cannot support a family are within legitimate state powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill treats the laws forbidding marriage without means as not exceeding state power; whether such laws are expedient depends on local circumstances, but they are defensible as interference to prevent social harm (e.g., overpopulation or poverty-induced social ills).
